sections.title: The Joke: Electricity Over IP
sections.content:
This is an April 1st, 2002 RFC published purely as humor. It proposes an absurd architecture called Mostly Pointless Lamp Switching (MPLampS) for carrying electricity over IP networks using an MPLS control plane.

The document is written in serious RFC style but with tongue firmly in cheek. Its stated purpose is to serve as a public service and template for anyone wishing to write ridiculous 'foo-over-MPLS' papers, treating the concept with exaggerated formality while the premise becomes increasingly absurd.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers wrote a silly pretend plan to send electricity like it was Internet data, using all the official terms, as a joke.

sections.title: The Fictional Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC defines an elaborate fictional vocabulary including Load-Switching Routers (LSRs) that replace transformers, Low-voltage Electricity Receptors (LERs) as light bulbs, and RSVP-TE (RSVP with Tariff Extensions) for establishing electricity paths in a deregulated environment. Voltages are equated to MPLS labels.

The architecture includes overlay and peer models for electricity consumption devices, multicast delivery for efficient broadcast of electricity, and even VPNs (Voltage Protected Networks) for customers wanting negligible voltage fluctuation.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke describes routers that control electricity like they control data packets, with official-sounding technical names for everything from light switches to power lines.

sections.title: The Satire Behind the Joke
sections.content:
The document parodies the IETF's 'Sub-IP' area initiative and the tendency of standards efforts to apply networking concepts to domains where they make no sense. It skewers marketing departments, overly complex specifications, and the tendency to write layer-on-layer of extension protocols to unrelated technologies.

The author openly acknowledges the absurdity: the RFC includes a 'Pre-requisite for reading' section advising readers to suppress their urge to ask if any of it makes sense, and defines key words that 'do not mean anything.' The work is presented as intentionally unimplementable, serving as a template for future silly proposal documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke pokes fun at how engineers sometimes try to make every new technology work over the Internet, even when it makes no sense to do so.
